video_title: Roman Storm's Retrial Delayed as Treasury’s Crypto Warning Looms
gist: On Unchained's 'Uneasy Money' show, hosts Kain Warwick and Taylor Monahan interview Coin Center executive director Peter Van Valkenburgh about four live US crypto-policy fronts: Treasury's Iran 'economic D-Day' secondary-sanctions release that names digital assets without carving out DeFi, the delayed Roman Storm retrial (now April 2027 pending a Rule 29 motion), the SEC's proposed 'Reg Crypto' ICO exemptions ($5M and $75M paths) as a hedge against a stalled Clarity Act, and whether the CFTC can build a compliant onshore path for a no-KYC perp DEX like Hyperliquid. The recurring argument: enforcement aimed at non-custodial code is ineffective and expensive, while immutability plus front-end compliance is emerging as the real regulatory dividing line.

themes.theme: Iran secondary sanctions and the crypto perimeter

insights.claim: Treasury's Iran secondary-sanctions release explicitly names digital assets and digital-asset intermediaries as potential targets but does not name DeFi, Uniswap, or any specific crypto project, and deliberately leaves no one a clear pass by claiming any source of the regime's illicit revenue could be targeted.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The absence of a DeFi carve-out is an open tail risk for protocol tokens, but the absence of a named target means no immediate, priceable enforcement event yet.
insights.quote: One doesn't normally announce D-Day before they have a D-day

insights.claim: The legally and constitutionally defensible targets for Iran secondary sanctions are custodial intermediaries with agency over funds — Iranian exchanges, front companies, money networks and brokers — not decentralized protocols.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Counterparty risk from this campaign concentrates in centralized offshore venues and OTC brokers rather than in on-chain protocol exposure.

insights.claim: The unruled-out extreme scenario is Treasury targeting non-custodial infrastructure — nodes, relayers, miners, or the software developers who make the networks possible — in an attempt to shut the networks down rather than police the humans using them.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: A low-probability, high-impact scenario worth monitoring in OFAC designations; it would reprice infrastructure and staking businesses, not just privacy tools.

insights.claim: An efficiency-maximizing Treasury will take out roughly 80% of viable sanctions-evasion avenues by targeting human brokers under a Pareto logic, because attacking a decentralized protocol produces poor bang-for-buck and enormous collateral damage.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: A pragmatism filter for handicapping enforcement headlines: ask whether the action increases interdiction per dollar, not whether it makes a statement.

insights.claim: The Treasury Secretary's claim of roughly $1 billion in seized Iranian crypto is doubted by an on-chain security researcher who tracks stablecoin freezes, because publicly traceable freezes have peaked in the hundreds of millions and were not attributed to Iran.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Discount headline enforcement totals; they likely aggregate years of actions and inflate the perceived on-chain reach of sanctions policy.
insights.quote: I was I was shocked to hear him just come out with this billion dollar number.

insights.claim: The concrete, verifiable Iran-linked freeze on record is roughly $344 million of USDT on Tron frozen in April across on the order of twenty wallets rather than a single address.
insights.speaker: hosts and guest citing a note from Laura Shin in the show chat
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic order of magnitude for stablecoin-issuer sanctions actions when sizing headline seizure claims.

insights.claim: Tether acts far more aggressively and more often than Circle when freezing addresses, and because freezes are instantly visible on a public chain they trigger a chase, making the timing and batching of freezes operationally critical.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Issuer freeze behavior is a differentiated operational risk between USDT and USDC that matters for anyone holding or routing size through either.

insights.claim: Blockchain analytics firms do not have magic attribution — effective sanctions interdiction requires a feedback loop combining human intelligence on the ground with exchanges, stablecoin issuers, bridges and custodians, all of whom can freeze.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for analytics vendors' capability claims and highlights that compliance value accrues to whoever aggregates cross-entity intelligence.

insights.claim: Address freezes produce false positives: some previously frozen wallets were subsequently unfrozen after mistakes were made.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Freeze-and-seize powers under new stablecoin rules carry real wrongful-seizure risk for legitimate holders and businesses.

insights.claim: Pushing Tether away from Washington and into a grey, US-avoidant posture produced worse enforcement outcomes than the current path, in which a less grey Tether becomes a more useful instrument of dollarization and sanctions leverage.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick)
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally more durable regulatory position for USDT in the US, reducing the tail risk previously priced into offshore-issuer dependence.

insights.claim: Cumulative crypto seized from Iran is trivial next to the campaign's other costs — the maritime blockade likely runs hundreds of millions of dollars a day and constrains single-digit billions of flows, making the crypto haul roughly eight hours' worth of Iranian oil money movement.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick)
insights.so_what: Crypto is a rounding error in this sanctions campaign, arguing against a large sustained enforcement push into on-chain rails.

insights.claim: The right strategic posture for American power is to accept that these networks cannot be regulated out of existence and instead legitimize as many businesses building on them as possible, so oversight lands where a human is still in the loop.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Frames the policy direction that favors licensed onshore crypto businesses over offshore grey markets, a tailwind for compliant US venues.
insights.quote: the best approach for America and American power globally is to embrace that these new technologies exist accept that they can't be regulated out of existence

themes.theme: GENIUS rulemaking and the stablecoin secondary market

insights.claim: The unresolved battleground in the Treasury and OCC rulemakings implementing the GENIUS Act is what obligations a stablecoin issuer owes on the secondary market — holders who received tokens wallet-to-wallet rather than by minting or redeeming with the issuer.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The single most consequential open item for stablecoin usability; watch the comment-period outcome before assuming permissionless transferability is safe.

insights.claim: Every GENIUS rulemaking so far has reiterated that issuers must have freeze-and-seize capability reaching into the secondary market but do NOT have to treat secondary-market holders as customers subject to full KYC and due diligence.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: If this balance holds, permissionless stablecoin transfer survives intact — the bull case for on-chain dollar volume — while freeze capability becomes a standard issuer feature.

insights.claim: Requiring issuers to identify every wallet holding their token would collapse the entire product rationale for stablecoins and force a for-profit company to collect intrusive personal data from people it owes no duties to.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Defines the specific regulatory outcome that would destroy stablecoin utility, giving investors a concrete trigger to watch in final rules.
insights.quote: you might as you might as well just be Venmo

insights.claim: The operative compliance surface for a decentralized exchange is its controlled front end, not the protocol — Uniswap's website has done sanctions compliance for a long time, as have Circle and Tether.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Front-end control is the enforceable chokepoint; protocol tokens whose teams run compliant interfaces face materially lower sanctions risk.

insights.claim: Public blockchains reduce the need for privileged information sharing in sanctions enforcement because flows to known sanctioned addresses can be watched in real time, and even privacy-oriented deployments like USDC on Aleo retain view keys.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Auditability is the argument that keeps public-chain stablecoins acceptable to Treasury; privacy chains that ship view keys inherit that defense.

themes.theme: Roman Storm retrial and developer liability

insights.claim: Roman Storm's retrial on the sanctions and money-laundering counts has been pushed from October to April 2027 while the judge rules on a Rule 29 motion that has now been pending about four months.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick) and Peter Van Valkenburgh
insights.so_what: Legal clarity on non-custodial developer liability is deferred by roughly six more months, extending the overhang on privacy-tool and infrastructure builders.

insights.claim: In the first trial the jury convicted Storm on the money-transmission count but hung on both the sanctions-evasion conspiracy and the money-laundering counts, which is a mistrial rather than an acquittal on those charges.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The surviving conviction is the one with the broadest read-across to any non-custodial builder, so the Rule 29 ruling matters more than the retrial date.

insights.claim: The central unresolved legal question is whether money transmission has a bright line at control of customer funds, or whether prosecutors can rely on SDNY's far vaguer theory that a frying pan does not hold the heat but transmits it.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: If the transmission test loses its custody bright line, every non-custodial protocol team in the US inherits unbounded licensing exposure.
insights.quote: I think they argued that a frying pan doesn't hold the heat, but it transmits the heat.

insights.claim: US sanctions law contains a statutory carve-out from the Berman amendments barring the president from sanctioning transactions in information, and courts have repeatedly rejected narrow readings of that exemption — a defense argument Coin Center pushes and almost nobody else discusses.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: An under-priced legal defense for software publishers; a favorable ruling on this theory would broadly de-risk US open-source crypto development.

insights.claim: There is no evidence Roman Storm ever made a transaction with a sanctioned party, so the sanctions count requires an over-broad conspiracy theory in which building a tool while knowing others might use it for evasion makes the developer a participant.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: If this conspiracy theory prevails at retrial, mere knowledge of illicit usage becomes actionable against any protocol team.

insights.claim: The Samurai Wallet case was distinguishable and harder to defend because of tweets welcoming new Russian oligarch users — public marketing of illicit use cases creates the bad facts that convict developers.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Operational security rule for token teams: marketing copy is discoverable evidence, and its absence is what makes the Storm defense stronger.
insights.quote: the really bad fact in that case were tweets about we welcome our new Russian oligarch users

insights.claim: Crypto teams marketing sanctions evasion as a growth use case — such as a protocol pitching 'new business use case' off the Iran news — are manufacturing evidence for prosecutors against themselves.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: A live behavioral red flag for diligence on privacy-adjacent token projects; such marketing measurably raises regulatory tail risk.
insights.quote: Like come on, man. I am begging you. I am begging you guys.

insights.claim: Tornado Cash volumes were measurably impacted by the OFAC sanctions but were not meaningfully impacted by Roman Storm's arrest and prosecution, showing that prosecuting a developer of an immutable contract does not reduce usage.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that developer prosecutions are ineffective policy — the strongest argument that this enforcement approach will eventually be abandoned.

insights.claim: North Korea never used Tornado Cash as a genuine off-ramp; it was just one of many layering steps, because laundering requires doing things — so removing it would not shift the front lines of DPRK finance.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Undercuts the national-security rationale for privacy-tool prosecutions and suggests future enforcement will refocus on asset recovery and threat-actor risk instead.

insights.claim: The most effective anti-hacking policy is immediately whacking down stolen funds and creating personal risk for threat actors through arrest, sanctions or ostracization, because that changes incentives — whereas taking down one mixing service does not recover funds or deter.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: A rubric for judging whether an enforcement action actually reduces protocol hack risk — the loss vector that most directly impairs on-chain asset values.

insights.claim: Prosecutors cited Coin Center's own explainers of how Tornado Cash works, before realizing Coin Center would become one of the parties suing the government to invalidate the sanctions.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Shows the government's technical understanding was thin and borrowed, weakening the 'they knew what they were doing' assumption behind the prosecution.

insights.claim: Tornado Cash was the first proof of concept to prove zero-knowledge cryptography at truly large volume outside Zcash, and its developer deserves hero rather than villain status for battle-testing the technology on Ethereum at great personal risk.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Frames on-chain privacy as an inevitable requirement for global finance, supporting long-horizon exposure to ZK infrastructure despite legal noise.
insights.quote: should be treated as as more of a hero than a villain, frankly

insights.claim: Prosecuting a developer cannot stop an immutable smart contract, so if the enforcement action does not stop the illicit financing it is a misallocation of scarce government resources better spent on human money-laundering networks.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The efficacy test that should eventually shift DOJ resourcing away from code and toward brokers, reducing developer-prosecution tail risk over time.
insights.quote: if the answer is no, because it's an immutable smart contract that if you throw Roman in jail for 30 years is still running, then what are you doing?

insights.claim: Only about three protocols have ever been simultaneously immutable, never hacked, and heavily used — Tornado Cash and Uniswap among them — and most teams no longer build immutably, which changes the legal conversation entirely.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan and Peter Van Valkenburgh
insights.so_what: Immutability functions as a scarce regulatory-defense moat; upgradeable protocols with admin keys face a materially different and worse legal posture.

insights.claim: At the time Tornado Cash launched, FinCEN's clearest-ever guidance said an anonymizing software provider is not a money transmitter, which is why firms like Cravath have called the money-transmission charge indefensible — there was no regulator to license with.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: A fair-notice argument that raises the odds of the money-transmission conviction being overturned on the Rule 29 motion or appeal.
insights.quote: an anonymizing software provider is not a money transmitter

insights.claim: For protocol builders the number one risk is still getting hacked, not the government, and a protocol's risk profile changes after launch as it attracts users and vulnerabilities the team never anticipated.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, security researcher
insights.so_what: Reorders diligence priorities for protocol investments: exploit risk dominates regulatory risk in expected-loss terms.
insights.quote: the number one risk is you getting hacked whenever you're building something

themes.theme: SEC 'Reg Crypto' exemptions vs a stalled Clarity Act

insights.claim: The SEC has proposed two crypto capital-raising exemptions: a one-time offering of up to $5 million over four years, and a second path allowing up to $75 million in any 12-month period, issued as a notice of proposed rulemaking with a 60-day comment period.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick) and Peter Van Valkenburgh
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term legal path back to compliant US token sales, reopening a primary-issuance market that has been effectively closed since 2018.

insights.claim: Reg Crypto descends directly from Hester Peirce's original safe-harbor proposal and conditions relief on legitimate designs on decentralization plus disclosures, so projects cannot take the money and deliver nothing.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Sets the qualifying bar for which token projects can access the exemption — running code and disclosure obligations, not pure narrative launches.

insights.claim: Legislation is preferable to rulemaking because a future commission can scrap its own rules while a future Congress must rewrite a statute, making the Clarity Act more valuable than Reg Crypto despite Reg Crypto arriving first.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Durability, not immediate permissiveness, is the metric for pricing regulatory-clarity news; rule-based relief carries political reversal risk.

insights.claim: If Reg Crypto survives Administrative Procedure Act 'arbitrary and capricious' challenges and real US investor money gets deployed under it, repeal becomes both economically and legally much harder — so adoption itself entrenches the rule.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Early adopters of the exemption create the constituency that makes it permanent; watch first-mover issuances as the signal that the regime has stuck.

insights.claim: TradFi incumbents are a plausible litigant against the SEC's new crypto rules, particularly on tokenized securities, rather than crypto firms being the ones in court.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Litigation risk to the new regime comes from incumbent finance defending its franchise — a headline risk for tokenization plays.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act has stalled in the Senate and presidential-ethics concerns about the Trump family's crypto interests may be an insurmountable barrier to passing it.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite near-term US crypto market-structure legislation; rulemaking is the realistic base case for the next legal milestones.
insights.quote: things like the presidential ethics concerns about the Trump family in crypto become an insurmountable barrier which I'm sorry to say might be true

insights.claim: Aggressive securities enforcement made honestly bootstrapping a network riskier than launching a joke token, so the perverse equilibrium is that teams still launch tokens but choose memecoins over funded network builds.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick)
insights.so_what: Explains the memecoin-dominated issuance mix as a regulatory artifact — a legal ICO path could rotate speculative flow back toward funded infrastructure.

insights.claim: The feared end state of restrictive token rules was VC-concentrated ownership, but the actual end state — memecoin launchpads where every Solana project is a memecoin — turned out far worse than a fund owning 30% of every project.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick)
insights.so_what: A blunt indictment of the current issuance market that argues capital-formation reform is the highest-leverage fix for token-market quality.
insights.quote: multicoin owning 30% of every Salana project seemed really bad at the time, but like every Salana project is a memecoin is a far worse end state to to land in.

insights.claim: The SAFT and Reg D era of 2017-2018 produced worse distribution than the unregulated ICOs it replaced — huge raises sold to accredited and foreign investors with no retail access, concentrating tokens in venture capital hands.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that compliance structures shape cap tables; token distribution quality should be diligenced as a function of the legal regime it launched under.

insights.claim: Ethereum's ICO raised roughly $30 million — small compared with the Reg D era raises that followed — yet produced the widest and most organically decentralized token distribution, alongside Bitcoin's fair launch.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The benchmark for judging distribution quality: raise size is inversely related to decentralization, a screen for evaluating new token launches.

themes.theme: Hyperliquid, perps and the CFTC jurisdictional gap

insights.claim: Hyperliquid was discussed by President Trump in a press conference with the CFTC named as the route to making it compliant, an unexpected elevation of a no-KYC perp DEX into US policy conversation.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick)
insights.so_what: Political sponsorship for onshoring a perp DEX is a material, underappreciated catalyst for the perp-DEX category and its tokens.

insights.claim: The binding legal obstacle to a compliant onshore perp DEX is that perps look like derivatives under CFTC plenary authority, and the eligible contract participant threshold of roughly $5 million is far stricter than the roughly $1 million accredited investor standard on the securities side.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Whether the CFTC crafts a retail carve-out is the single gating item for a US-legal perp DEX; without it, compliance means institutional-only access.

insights.claim: The CFTC has authority over commodity derivatives but not over the spot markets that price them, leaving a structural blind spot for manipulation that the Clarity Act was designed to close in digital commodities.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: With Clarity stalled, no regulator supervises crypto spot markets — a persistent manipulation risk and a reason venue consolidation under one regulator stays blocked.

insights.claim: The CFTC's historic mandate is market-manipulation supervision, data collection and fair efficient markets, not KYC — anti-money-laundering at financial institutions has always been Treasury's job, so a venue could in principle be supervised for manipulation without bank-grade identity requirements.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The legal path to a supervised no-KYC perp venue is not foreclosed, contradicting the market's assumption that CFTC registration necessarily means mandatory KYC.

insights.claim: The correct regulatory frame is to target a specific public-policy problem — money laundering versus market manipulation — rather than to regulate a technology, and pseudonyms or zero-knowledge proofs could satisfy market supervision without identity disclosure.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Points to a hybrid compliance architecture where ZK identity/attestation infrastructure becomes the enabling layer for regulated permissionless venues.

insights.claim: Uniswap has been de facto grandfathered as an unregulated no-KYC venue because its pools are immutable infrastructure, giving it a golden legitimacy claim that regulating pipes is not the same as regulating a delivery van service.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Immutability plus a spot-only product is the template that has survived regulatory attention; derivative venues cannot simply copy it.
insights.quote: you'd be crazy to think that we should, you know, regulate pipes the same way we regulate a delivery van service

insights.claim: This CFTC is effectively claiming authority over all gaming by reasoning that any payout contingent on a future event is a derivative, which sweeps in essentially everything.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: A rapidly expanding CFTC perimeter into prediction markets and gaming — regulatory tailwind for licensed event-contract venues and a headwind for state-regulated gambling incumbents.

insights.claim: Rulemaking fights become wars of attrition: once regulations are in place and real markets operate under them, tearing them away has economic consequences for Americans, so incumbency in the rules favors whoever gets in first.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: First movers under new crypto rules capture durable regulatory advantage even before the litigation resolves.

insights.claim: The fragmentation of US financial regulation across roughly seven federal regulators plus state money-transmitter licensing acts as a check that capped the damage even under the most hostile SEC regime, unlike a single unified authority such as the UK's.
insights.speaker: host (Kain Warwick) and Peter Van Valkenburgh
insights.so_what: US jurisdictional messiness is a structural downside protection for crypto businesses versus single-regulator jurisdictions — relevant to domicile choice.

insights.claim: The DOJ's siloed structure explains why SDNY continues pressing the Tornado Cash prosecution despite the administration's stated policy of ending regulation by prosecution, because SDNY sees itself as the global financial cop with jurisdiction over transnational crime.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: Pro-crypto federal policy does not automatically neutralize individual prosecutor offices — venue-specific legal risk persists regardless of headline policy shifts.

insights.claim: A 2025-era DOJ memo committed to ending regulation by prosecution by dropping unlicensed money-transmission cases against parties that fit FinCEN guidance saying non-custodial actors are not money transmitters, the same pivot that coincided with a serious push against cartel money brokers.
insights.speaker: Peter Van Valkenburgh, Coin Center executive director
insights.so_what: The stated federal policy baseline against which any new action on non-custodial crypto should be judged as an outlier.
